title: The Cyclades: a dialect patchwork shaped by the Venetian dukes
lead: The Cyclades look alike on a postcard, but their speech does not. On one island the **γ** vanishes (**ο έρος** for **ο γέρος**), on another **κ** becomes **τσ** (**τσέρατο** for **κέρατο**), and on Andros and Tinos you will even hear northern vowels. The islands were held for three and a half centuries by Venetian and other Latin lords of the **Duchy of the Archipelago**, who left Italian words, Catholic villages and castles behind. Since the 19th century, islanders have moved to Athens and Piraeus, and the dialects have been fading for a long time; they are still among the least studied in Greece.
facts: Kea, Kythnos, Serifos, Sifnos, Kimolos, Milos, Paros, Naxos, Syros, Antiparos, Sikinos, Folegandros, Ios, Santorini, Anafi, Andros, Tinos, Mykonos, Amorgos and the Small Cyclades.

1) southern vowels, close to Cretan (most islands); 2) close to the Dodecanese (Amorgos, Donousa, Irakleia, Schinoussa, Koufonisia); 3) northern vowels (parts of Andros and Tinos); 4) semi-northern (Mykonos). Sifnos sits between 1 and 2.

Santorini, Milos, perhaps Anafi: southern, with Crete. Central Cyclades (Amorgos, Irakleia…), western (Sifnos, Kimolos, Serifos), Mykonos on its own, and a northern Cyclades group (Andros, Tinos, Kea, Kythnos, Syros, Naxos, Paros, Ios, Folegandros).
Duchy of the Archipelago (1207–1579), Ottoman rule to 1821, part of Greece from 1830.
Receding already in studies of the 1920s–30s; few modern descriptions.

timeline.text: Arab raids empty many smaller islands; settlement shrinks to fortified hilltop villages.

After the Fourth Crusade, the Venetian Marco Sanudo founds the **Duchy of the Archipelago** with its capital at Naxos. Latin lords rule most of the Cyclades; Tinos and Mykonos stay Venetian, Tinos until 1715.
The **Frankokratia**. A Catholic Latin aristocracy rules a Greek Orthodox peasantry. Italian words enter everyday speech, and Catholic communities form on Syros, Tinos and Naxos that still exist.
The Ottomans take the islands; the Duchy ends in 1579. Islands keep a good deal of local self-government.
Refugees from Chios and Psara found **Ερμούπολη** on Syros, for a time the largest port of free Greece.
Emigration to Athens, Piraeus and the mines of Lavrion. Later, tourism and Standard Greek complete the change.

sections.after: Standard Greek does not allow stress further back than the third syllable from the end. Cycladic **ήκαμενε** breaks that rule, and many speakers 'repair' it with a second stress: **ήκαμενέ**.

sections.h: Mykonos, Andros and Tinos: the northern islands of the south
sections.text: Mykonos is the one Cycladic island with **semi-northern** vowels: unstressed **ου** and **ι** may drop, while **ε** and **ο** stay. Parts of Andros and Tinos go further, with fully **northern** vowel loss of the kind heard in Thessaly or Macedonia. One suggested reason is settlement: northern Andros received Albanian-speaking (Arvanite) settlers in the late Middle Ages, and the northern Cyclades had close links with Euboea and the mainland. The result is a reminder that a dialect map follows the movements of people, not the shape of the sea.

culture.text: Syros and Tinos still have large Catholic communities, a legacy of the Duchy: Ano Syros, above Ermoupoli, has a Catholic cathedral, and many Tinian villages have both an Orthodox and a Catholic church. Across the islands the summer **πανηγύρι**, with violin and **τσαμπούνα** bagpipe, is where you are most likely to hear old dialect songs and **κοτσάκια**, the rhyming couplets of Naxos.
